run.request: Our team of six runs everything through email and a shared spreadsheet. We want to move to a shared task tool in two weeks without dropping any client work. Give us a plan for choosing the tool, moving the work over, and getting everyone to actually use it.
run.title: Move your team of six from email and a spreadsheet to a shared task tool in two weeks
run.goal: You can pick a task tool, move every open client job into it, and get all six people working in it within 14 days without missing a deadline.
run.summary: You can switch your team of six to a shared task tool in 14 days. Use 4 days to test 3 tools and pick one. Use 5 days to move every open client job over, with one migration owner checking that nothing is missing. Use the last days to set six team rules and hold short daily check-ins. The spreadsheet and email stay your real record until the sheet is frozen at the end of day 9. If the checks show gaps, the freeze can slip to day 12 at the latest, so client deadlines never depend on the tool going live on time.

body.text: Use day 1 to write down what the tool must do. The migration owner and one other teammate should spend about an hour on it. Any tool that misses a must-have is out, however good it looks.

items: Every task has one owner and a due date, with reminders before it is due.
You can forward a client email into the tool and it becomes a task, or links to one.
You can see all work for one client or project on a single screen.
You can import a CSV file, so you can bring tasks over from your spreadsheet.
It has a working mobile app for checking and updating tasks away from the desk.
Six people fit inside $0 to $90 a month (estimate), billed monthly so you can leave.
Optional: comments and file attachments on each task, so status talk can move out of email.

body.text: Also on day 1, pick one tool of each kind in the table below. That gives you a shortlist of 3. Check each one's pricing page that day, because plans and free limits change often. The prices in the table are estimates.

items: Day 2: sign up for free trials of all 3 tools. Two people each add the same 10 real open client tasks to every tool. They also forward 2 real client emails into each one and set owners and due dates. These trial tasks are copies. The sheet and email stay the real record.
Day 3: the other four people log in on desktop and phone. In each tool, each person finds their own tasks, updates one, leaves a comment and marks one done. That takes about 20 minutes per tool.

Day 4: all six fill in the score sheet below for each tool, which takes about 10 minutes in total. Add up the scores. The highest total wins unless that tool failed a must-have. If two tools are within 3 points of each other, pick the cheaper one. Decide by the end of day 4 and pay for the first month.

body.text: For the score sheet, each person rates each tool from 1 (poor) to 5 (great) on five lines. It was easy to find my own tasks. Email to task worked without fuss. The client view showed what I needed. The phone app was usable. I would open this every morning. The top score is 25 per person and 150 for the team. Each person also writes down one thing they disliked about each tool, so the rollout can deal with it.

sections.heading: Days 5 to 9: move the work over

body.text: Before day 5, name one migration owner. Pick the person who can give 3 to 5 hours a week. They clean the sheet, run the import and check every day that the sheet and the tool match. Everyone else keeps doing client work as usual.

items: Make a copy of the spreadsheet and name it with today's date. This is your backup. Save it before you archive anything.
Sort the sheet by status. Move every finished or cancelled row to a new tab called Archive. Don't import these rows.
Read each open row. Close any row that is done but was never marked done. If you aren't sure, ask the owner.
Make sure every open row has a client name, a short task title, one owner and a due date. Leave the date blank only if the work truly has no deadline.
Merge any duplicate rows. Split any row that holds more than one job into one row per job.

body.text: Day 6: import the open tasks. If you have more than about 40 open rows, save the cleaned tab as a CSV file and use the tool's import feature. Import 5 rows first and check that owners and dates came through correctly, then import the rest. With 40 rows or fewer, typing them in by hand is often just as fast, at about 1 to 2 hours (estimate). Either way, add a column to the sheet called "In tool" and mark each row yes once its task exists.
Days 7 to 9: run both systems side by side.

items: From day 7, every new client request goes into the tool first. Add it to the sheet as well, only so the sheet stays complete.
Each morning, the migration owner counts the open rows in the sheet and the open tasks in the tool. If the counts differ, find the missing job and add it the same day.
When a status changes, update the tool. In the sheet, only the "In tool" mark needs to be right.
The migration owner also runs the daily 15-minute inbox scan described in the safety net section, to catch any job that never made it into the sheet.

body.text: Freeze the sheet at the end of day 9. Before you lock it, every open row must show yes in the "In tool" column and the counts must match. Then set the sheet to view only for everyone. Add a note in the first row: "Read only. All work is in the task tool." Keep the sheet for at least 30 days for reference. If the counts still don't match on day 9, push the freeze back 1 to 3 days. Don't lock a sheet that still has gaps.

sections.heading: Days 8 to 14: get everyone to use it

body.text: Hold the kickoff on day 8, once the open jobs are in the tool. From then on, the tool is where your team works. Until the sheet is frozen at the end of day 9, new requests still go into both the sheet and the tool. Agree on these six rules at the kickoff and pin them at the top of the tool.

items: Every client request becomes a task within one working day. If it came by email, forward it into the tool or paste the key lines into the task.
Every task has exactly one owner and a due date. Others can help, but only one name is on it.
Status talk happens in the task, not in email or chat. If you answer a teammate by email, copy the answer into the task.
Clients still email you as normal. Reply to them by email, then log anything that changes the work in the task.
Before you finish each day, update your own tasks. Mark them done, move the due date or add a one-line note.
If it's not in the tool, it's not on the list. No side lists, and no new rows in the spreadsheet after the freeze.

body.text: Daily check-in, days 9 to 13: 10 minutes at the same time each morning, standing up or on a call. Open the tool on a shared screen and look at three things: tasks due today or overdue, tasks with no owner or no date, and anything someone is stuck on. Fix gaps on the spot. Don't try to do the work itself in the meeting. If things look clean after day 14, cut the check-in to two or three times a week.

If someone keeps slipping back to email, start small and stay friendly. The first time, just turn their email into a task and reply with the link. The second time, have a quick private chat and ask what's getting in the way. Usually it's a missing view, too many notifications or a phone app that was never set up. Those take about 10 minutes to fix. If it keeps happening after day 11, pair them with the person who uses the tool most for one working session. Keep it out of the group check-in and the day 14 review, and never name anyone there.

Day 14 review, 30 to 45 minutes: count overdue tasks, tasks with no owner and client requests that skipped the tool. Ask each person for one thing that works and one thing that annoys them. Then decide whether to keep, change or drop each rule, and agree on at most two changes to the setup. Set a short follow-up review for day 30.

sections.heading: Keeping client work safe during the switch

body.text: Two rules keep client work safe. First, the migration owner runs the calendar below and does the row-by-row checks. Second, the sheet and email stay the only real record until the freeze at the end of day 9. Until then, treat the new tool as a draft. That includes the real tasks added during the trial.
The biggest risks, and the fix for each:

items: Lost tasks: a job sits in the sheet but never makes it into the tool. Fix: the dated backup on day 5 and the full match on day 9. A job counts as moved only after its owner confirms it.

Missed emails: a client request lands in someone's inbox during the switch and nobody records it. Fix: from day 7 to day 13, the migration owner spends 15 minutes a day comparing that day's client emails against new tasks. Any request without a task gets one before the end of the day.

Double entry: from day 7 to day 9, new requests go into both the sheet and the tool. That takes extra time, and the two records can drift apart. Fix: keep this window to 3 working days and use the "In tool" mark. Double entry stops at the freeze.

One holdout: one person keeps working from email or a private list, so nobody sees their jobs. Fix: from day 10, the migration owner checks that person's open jobs against the tool every day. Anything missing goes in with that person as the owner. Then follow the steps in the adoption section: a private chat first, then pairing.

Deadline clash: a client deadline falls during the busiest days of the switch. Fix: on day 5, list every client deadline due between day 5 and day 16. On day 6, before the import, check that every job on that list is in the import file with its owner and due date.

body.text: Signs the plan is slipping: no tool is chosen by the end of day 4. The day 9 match finds more than 5 open jobs missing, or a missing job is due in the next 7 days. More than 10 percent of tasks have no owner or no due date. A client chases you for work that should already be tracked.

When to push the freeze: if any of these signs shows up on day 9, push the freeze back 1 to 3 days, to the end of day 12 at the latest. Double entry continues until the new freeze. Rerun the full match on the new freeze day, before the sheet goes read-only. Keep the day 14 review on the calendar either way. If you can't freeze by the end of day 12, use the review to set a firm new date. Don't let the sheet and the tool run side by side with no end date.

assumptions: Your budget is modest: an estimated $0 to $15 per person per month, or $0 to $90 a month for six people.
No one works full time on the switch. One person, the migration owner, can give about 3 to 5 hours a week.
Your spreadsheet holds roughly 30 to 150 open tasks or client jobs.
Client work keeps running the whole time, and clients still reach you by email.
The tools you shortlist offer free trials long enough to cover days 2 to 4.
Prices and free plan limits are estimates and change often, so check them on day 1.
checks: The day ranges in each section fit together and the full plan ends by day 14.
Every open client job from the spreadsheet has a clear path into the tool, and one named person checks that nothing is missing before the sheet is frozen.
Price figures are labeled as estimates, given as ranges, and multiplied out for six people.
The team rules are specific enough to check, for example every task has an owner and a due date.
The page names a fallback if the switch slips, so client deadlines don't depend on the tool going live on time.
conflicts: Trial data: choose-tool puts 10 real open client tasks and real emails into the trials. Safety-net says testers log no real client work in the trial.
Scoring: choose-tool has all six score on day 4. Safety-net has testers fill in score sheets on day 3.
Backup copy: move-work makes it on day 5. Safety-net makes it on day 4.
Sheet cleanup: move-work has the migration owner clean and archive on day 5. Safety-net has all six mark rows on day 5 and archives on day 6.
Freeze slip: move-work allows 1 to 3 days. Safety-net allows 2 to 3 days, to day 12 or 13.
Day 9 match time: move-work gives 30 to 45 minutes. Safety-net gives 1 to 3 hours.
Spreadsheet rows: get-adoption allows no new rows after the day 8 kickoff. Move-work and safety-net keep double entry through day 9.
Import order: move-work imports all open tasks on day 6. Safety-net holds back jobs with near deadlines and moves them last.
Inbox check: move-work spot-checks 5 tasks a day on days 7 to 9. Safety-net scans all client email for 15 minutes a day on days 7 to 13.
Holdout handling: get-adoption pairs the person with a strong user after day 11 and names no one in group meetings. Safety-net raises it in the day 14 review.
Role name: the same person is called "migration owner" in move-work, "switch lead" in safety-net and "tool owner" in get-adoption.
